etymology: Matthew, from Hebrew Mattithyah, gift of the LORD; also called Levi, son of Alphaeus; the publican called to be an apostle.
biblical_def: Matthew, also called Levi the son of Alphaeus, was a publican—a Jewish tax-gatherer in the service of Rome, a class despised as traitors and extortioners—whom the Lord Jesus called from the receipt of custom with the single word, Follow me. He rose, left all, and followed (Luke 5:27-28), and made a great feast in his house, gathering publicans and sinners to hear the Physician who came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance. Matthew became one of the twelve apostles and, by the church’s constant testimony, the writer of the first Gospel, which presents Jesus as the promised Son of David and King of the Jews, the fulfilment of the law and the prophets, citing the Hebrew Scriptures more than any other evangelist. The call of Matthew is a standing proof of sovereign grace, that Christ chooses the unlikely and the outcast, and that no trade or reputation is too low for the effectual call. The dictionary honors Matthew as apostle and evangelist, the despised publican made a steward of the gospel, whose pen records the King and His kingdom for the church of every age.
webster_summary: The publican Levi, son of Alphaeus, called from the receipt of custom to be an apostle and, by the church’s testimony, writer of the first Gospel.
webster_full: MATTHEW LEVI, the publican called to be an apostle of Christ.
A Jewish tax-gatherer for Rome, of the despised class of publicans.
Called from the receipt of custom with the word, Follow me (Mat 9:9).
Author, by the church’s testimony, of the first Gospel.
Presents Jesus as the Son of David, King, and fulfilment of the prophets.
scriptures: Mat 9:9
And as Jesus passed forth from thence, he saw a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him.
Luk 5:28

Mar 2:17

corruption_summary: The call of Matthew is sentimentalized into a tale of self-acceptance; in truth it is sovereign grace summoning a sinner out of his sin to follow.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to resist is the sentimental reading that turns Matthew’s call into a parable of self-acceptance—Jesus affirming the publican as he was, with no demand of repentance or forsaking. But the text says he left all, rose up, and followed (Luke 5:28), and that Christ came to call sinners to repentance (Mark 2:17). Grace did not leave Matthew at his table; it called him from it. The feast he made was not a celebration of the old life but a gathering of the lost to meet the Physician.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond this sentimental drift. The principle to recover is the nature of the effectual call: it is sovereign, free, and transforming. Christ chose a despised tax-gatherer, not because Matthew first cleaned himself, but because the Lord delights to show mercy to the unworthy. The call that summoned Matthew is the same call that summons every sinner—not Follow me when you are ready, but Follow me, with the power to make the dead rise and obey.

etymology: Greek Philippos, lover of horses; one of the seven, called the evangelist to distinguish him from the apostle Philip.
biblical_def: Philip the Evangelist was one of the seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, chosen by the early church to serve tables that the apostles might give themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word (Acts 6:3-5). He is called the evangelist to distinguish him from Philip the apostle. When persecution scattered the church from Jerusalem, Philip went down to Samaria and preached Christ there, and the city had great joy; and being directed by the angel and the Spirit, he met the Ethiopian eunuch upon the desert road, opened the Scripture of Isaiah to him, preached unto him Jesus, and baptized him, that the gospel might go to the ends of the earth (Acts 8). He had four daughters who prophesied, and he later lodged Paul at Caesarea. Philip stands as a model of the gospel-bearer: faithful in lowly service, ready at the Spirit’s bidding, mighty in opening the Scriptures to the seeking soul, and instant to baptize the believer. The dictionary honors Philip the Evangelist as a pattern of evangelistic obedience, who proved that the deacon’s table and the desert road are alike fields for the preaching of Christ.
webster_summary: One of the seven, called the evangelist; preached Christ in Samaria and to the Ethiopian eunuch, a pattern of Spirit-led, Scripture-opening evangelism.
webster_full: PHILIP THE EVANGELIST, one of the seven of Acts 6, full of the Holy Ghost.
Distinguished from Philip the apostle by the title evangelist.
Preached Christ in Samaria with great joy when the church was scattered.
Met the Ethiopian eunuch, opened Isaiah, preached Jesus, and baptized him.
Had four daughters who prophesied; lodged Paul at Caesarea.
scriptures: Act 8:5
Then Philip went down to the city of Samaria, and preached Christ unto them.
Act 8:35
Then Philip opened his mouth, and began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus.
Act 8:12
But when they believed Philip preaching the things concerning the kingdom of God, and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women.
Act 21:8

corruption_summary: Philip’s ministry is read as freelance enthusiasm; in truth it was Spirit-led, Scripture-grounded, Christ-centered preaching in the church’s order.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The danger is rather to read Philip’s desert encounter as a model of freelance, experience-driven religion, as though the Spirit’s leading bypassed the word. The text shows the opposite: when Philip met the eunuch, he began at the same scripture of Isaiah and preached unto him Jesus (Acts 8:35). The Spirit who arranged the meeting also bound the message to the written word and to the crucified Christ it foretold.

The principle to recover is the marriage of Spirit and Scripture in evangelism. Philip was full of the Holy Ghost (Acts 6:3), yet his evangelism was the opening of the prophet’s scroll and the preaching of the name of Jesus, followed by baptism upon profession of faith (Acts 8:12). True evangelism is neither cold lecture nor unmoored enthusiasm, but the Spirit-empowered preaching of Christ from the Scriptures. Philip shows that the lowliest servant, ready at the Lord’s bidding, may carry the gospel to a stranger and so to a continent.
roots_summary: Greek Philippos, lover of horses; the evangelist among the seven, who preached Christ in Samaria and to the Ethiopian eunuch.

etymology: Saul, Hebrew Sha’ul, asked of God; of Tarsus in Cilicia, the birthplace of the apostle Paul before his conversion.
biblical_def: Saul of Tarsus is the name of the apostle Paul before and at his conversion—a Hebrew of the Hebrews, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee taught at the feet of Gamaliel, zealous toward God and blameless as touching the righteousness of the law, who became the chief persecutor of the church. He consented to the death of Stephen, made havock of the church, haling men and women to prison, and breathing out threatenings and slaughter, set out for Damascus with letters to bind the disciples there. On that road, at noon, a light from heaven above the brightness of the sun shone round him, and the risen Christ arrested His enemy: Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? Struck down and blinded, Saul was led by the hand into the city, and after three days, by the ministry of Ananias, received sight, was filled with the Spirit, and was baptized. The persecutor became the apostle to the Gentiles, the chiefest of sinners made the pattern of long-suffering grace (1 Tim 1:15-16). The dictionary honors the conversion of Saul as the supreme monument of sovereign, conquering grace, that lays hold of the rebel in mid-rebellion and makes him the bondservant of the Lord he assailed.
webster_summary: The name of the apostle Paul before conversion; the zealous Pharisee and persecutor arrested by the risen Christ on the Damascus road.
webster_full: SAUL OF TARSUS, the apostle Paul before and at his conversion.
A Pharisee of Benjamin, taught by Gamaliel, blameless in the law’s righteousness.
Consented to Stephen’s death and made havock of the church.
Arrested by the risen Christ on the Damascus road: why persecutest thou me?
Blinded, then by Ananias received sight, the Spirit, and baptism.
scriptures: Act 9:4
And he fell to the earth, and heard a voice saying unto him, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?
Act 9:1
And Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went unto the high priest,
This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.
Gal 1:23
But they had heard only, That he which persecuted us in times past now preacheth the faith which once he destroyed.
corruption_summary: Saul’s conversion is psychologized into an inner crisis resolved; Scripture presents the objective intervention of the risen Christ upon His enemy.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to resist is the psychologizing of Saul’s conversion into a subjective crisis—a guilt-ridden zealot working through inner conflict until he reframes his beliefs. The text allows no such reading. Saul was not seeking; he was breathing out threatenings and slaughter (Acts 9:1), armed with letters to imprison the saints, when a light above the sun struck him down and a living voice named his sin: why persecutest thou me? (Acts 9:4). The conversion was not the climax of his searching but the interruption of his rebellion.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond this psychologizing drift. The principle to recover is the sovereignty and objectivity of saving grace. Christ did not wait for Saul to soften; He conquered His enemy in mid-assault and made him a chosen vessel. This is why Paul calls himself the chief of sinners and the pattern of Christ’s long-suffering (1 Tim 1:15-16): if grace could lay hold of the persecutor, it can lay hold of any. The road to Damascus is the abiding proof that conversion is the work of God, not the achievement of man.
roots_summary: Saul (asked of God) of Tarsus; the Pharisee and persecutor whom the risen Christ arrested and made the apostle to the Gentiles.
roots_lines: Saul — Hebrew Sha’ul, asked of God; of Tarsus in Cilicia.

The chief of sinners made the apostle to the Gentiles (1Ti 1:15).

etymology: From women + disciple; the faithful women who followed and ministered to Christ and the apostles.
biblical_def: The women disciples were the company of faithful women who followed the Lord Jesus, ministered to Him of their substance, stood by His cross when the men had fled, watched the sepulchre, and were the first witnesses of His resurrection. Luke names Mary called Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna, and many others, who followed Him out of Galilee and ministered unto Him of their substance (Luke 8:2-3). They followed Him to Calvary and beheld where He was laid; and to them first the risen Christ appeared, sending them to tell His brethren—so that women carried the first word of the resurrection to the apostles. In the early church, women such as Mary the mother of John Mark, Lydia, Priscilla, Dorcas, and Phoebe served Christ in prayer, hospitality, instruction of women, works of mercy, and the support of the gospel. Scripture honors their devotion without overturning the order God appointed: the office of elder is reserved to qualified men (1 Tim 2:12; 3:1-7), while the labors of godly women are essential, honored, and dear to Christ. The dictionary celebrates the women disciples as a chief glory of the gospel—last at the cross, first at the tomb—and rebukes both the world that despises them and the error that would erase the order in which their service shines.
webster_summary: The faithful women who followed and ministered to Christ; last at the cross, first at the tomb, and witnesses of the resurrection, honored within God’s appointed order.
webster_full: WOMEN DISCIPLES, the faithful women who followed and ministered to Christ.
Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna, and many others ministered of their substance.
Stood by the cross when the men had fled; watched the sepulchre.
First witnesses of the resurrection, sent to tell the apostles.
Honored within God’s order: eldership reserved to qualified men (1Ti 2:12).

corruption_summary: The women disciples are seized by egalitarians to overturn male eldership and dismissed by others as marginal; Scripture honors them within the order God set.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to resist is the egalitarian seizure of the women disciples as a proof-text against the order God has appointed. Because faithful women followed Christ, ministered to Him, and first announced His resurrection, the argument runs that male-only eldership must fall. But devotion and office are not the same thing. The Lord who was served by these women is the same Lord whose apostle, writing by the Spirit, reserves the teaching-and-ruling office of elder to qualified men (1 Tim 2:12; 3:1-7). To honor the women disciples is not to erase that order but to see their service shine within it.

The opposite corruption despises or marginalizes these women, as though their service were a lesser footnote. Scripture does the reverse: it records that they stood by the cross when the men had fled (Matt 27:55), that the risen Christ appeared first to them and sent them to the apostles (John 20:18), and that women like Phoebe were commended servants of the church (Rom 16:1). The dictionary celebrates the women disciples without adopting the egalitarian framing, and recovers the truth that God’s order and the honor of godly women are not enemies but friends—the order is the very setting in which their devotion is most beautiful.
roots_summary: Women + disciple; the faithful women who followed and ministered to Christ, honored as witnesses of the resurrection within God’s appointed order.
roots_lines: Women disciples — the faithful women who followed and served Christ.

etymology: From restoration + Peter; the risen Christ’s recommissioning of the apostle who had denied Him.
biblical_def: The restoration of Peter is the tender scene by the Sea of Tiberias in which the risen Christ recovers the apostle who had denied Him thrice. Peter, who had boasted that though all men forsook the Lord he would not, had, in the high priest’s courtyard, denied with oaths that he knew the man, and gone out and wept bitterly. After the resurrection, the Lord met him by the lake and asked three times, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?—a threefold question answering the threefold denial—and to each confession of love commissioned him afresh: Feed my lambs; feed my sheep. Peter was grieved that He asked the third time, yet appealed to the Lord’s own knowledge: thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee. So the fallen apostle was not cast off but restored, recommissioned to feed the flock and forewarned of the death by which he would glorify God. The restoration of Peter is the gospel for backsliders: that the Lord who foreknew the fall also prayed that Peter’s faith should not fail, and that genuine love to Christ, however it has stumbled, is met with full forgiveness and renewed trust. The dictionary honors this scene as the pattern of Christ’s dealing with His fallen but truly loving servants.
webster_summary: The risen Christ’s recovery of Peter after his threefold denial; a threefold question of love answered with a threefold commission to feed the flock.
webster_full: RESTORATION OF PETER, the risen Christ’s recovery of the denying apostle.
Peter had denied Christ thrice and gone out and wept bitterly.
By the Sea of Tiberias, Christ asked three times, Lovest thou me?
Each confession of love met with a commission: Feed my sheep.
The gospel for backsliders: genuine love to Christ met with forgiveness.
scriptures: So when they had dined, Jesus saith to Simon Peter, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these? He saith unto him, Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my lambs.

He saith unto him the third time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? Peter was grieved because he said unto him the third time, Lovest thou me? And he said unto him, Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee. Jesus saith unto him, Feed my sheep.
But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren.
And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.
corruption_summary: Peter’s restoration is read as mere therapeutic affirmation; in truth it is repentance met by sovereign grace and a renewed call to costly service.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The danger is the therapeutic flattening of the scene into a tale of self-forgiveness and emotional healing, as if the point were Peter’s recovered self-esteem. The text is sterner and sweeter than that. The threefold question probed Peter to grief (John 21:17), recalling his threefold denial, and the restoration issued not in comfort alone but in a costly commission to feed the flock and a forewarning of martyrdom.

The principle to recover is the gospel for the backslider. Peter’s fall was real and grievous, yet the Lord had prayed that his faith should not fail and that, once converted, he should strengthen his brethren (Luke 22:32). Restoration came not because Peter excused himself but because he loved Christ and cast himself on the Lord’s own knowledge: thou knowest that I love thee. Christ does not cast off the servant who truly loves Him and has stumbled; He restores, recommissions, and uses him. This is hope for every fallen saint who would return.
roots_summary: Restoration + Peter; the risen Christ’s threefold recommissioning of the apostle who had thrice denied Him.
roots_lines: Restoration of Peter — the risen Christ’s recovery of the denier.
Peter had denied Christ thrice and wept bitterly (Luk 22:62).

The pattern of Christ’s dealing with His fallen but loving servants.
usage: The restoration of Peter answers his threefold denial with a threefold question of love.
Christ recommissioned the fallen apostle to feed His lambs and His sheep.
It is the gospel for backsliders who truly love the Lord they have failed.

etymology: From Paul + imprisonment; the apostle’s bonds for the gospel, especially at Caesarea and Rome.
biblical_def: Paul’s imprisonment refers to the apostle’s repeated bonds for the gospel of Christ—his arrest at Jerusalem, his two years held at Caesarea under Felix and Festus, his appeal to Caesar, his voyage and shipwreck, and his imprisonment at Rome, where, though chained to a soldier, he dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, preaching the kingdom of God and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ with all confidence, no man forbidding him (Acts 28:30-31). From these bonds came the prison epistles—Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, and Philemon—in which Paul calls himself the prisoner of Jesus Christ, declares that the things which happened to him fell out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel, and rejoices that his bonds in Christ were manifest in all the palace. He learned in whatsoever state he was therewith to be content, and proved that the word of God is not bound though the preacher be. Paul’s imprisonment is the great testimony that the gospel advances through suffering, that Christ is magnified in the bonds of His servants, and that no chain can silence the word. The dictionary honors his bonds as a crown, and his prison letters as a treasury wrung from affliction for the comfort and instruction of the church.
webster_summary: The apostle’s bonds for the gospel at Caesarea and Rome, from which came the prison epistles and the testimony that the word of God is not bound.
webster_full: PAUL'S IMPRISONMENT, the apostle’s bonds for the gospel of Christ.

Dwelt two years at Rome, preaching the kingdom, no man forbidding him.
From these bonds came Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, and Philemon.
Proved the gospel advances through suffering, and the word is not bound.
scriptures: Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, no man forbidding him.
Php 1:12
But I would ye should understand, brethren, that the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel;
Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
Eph 3:1
For this cause I Paul, the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles,
corruption_summary: Paul’s bonds are read as a setback or a sign of failed mission; Scripture shows them as the furtherance of the gospel and the magnifying of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the worldly instinct that reads imprisonment as defeat, as though the chaining of the apostle proved the failure of his mission or the absence of God’s favor. Paul himself overturns this judgment: the things which happened to him fell out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel (Phil 1:12), his bonds in Christ were manifest throughout the palace, and the word of God, he insists, is not bound though he be (2 Tim 2:9).

The principle to recover is the divine pattern that the gospel advances through the suffering of its servants. From a prison cell Paul wrote the letters that have fed the church for two thousand years; from his chains the praetorian guard heard the name of Christ; from his afflictions he taught the saints contentment in every state. Suffering is not the contradiction of fruitful ministry but often its very furnace. The Lord magnifies Christ in the bonds of His servants and proves that no power of man can silence His word.
roots_summary: Paul + imprisonment; the apostle’s bonds for the gospel, from which came the prison epistles and the testimony that the word is not bound.
roots_lines: Paul’s imprisonment — the apostle’s bonds for the gospel.
Two years at Caesarea; appeal to Caesar; two years at Rome.

The word of God is not bound, though the preacher be (2Ti 2:9).
usage: Paul’s imprisonment fell out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel.

The word of God is not bound, though its preacher be in chains.

etymology: From son + Abraham; a title of natural descent and, more deeply, of the faith that reckons one a true child of the patriarch.
biblical_def: A son of Abraham is, in the first sense, a natural descendant of the patriarch through Isaac and Jacob, an Israelite according to the flesh. But Scripture presses the title to a deeper meaning: the true sons of Abraham are not merely those of his blood but those of his faith. They which are of faith, the same are the children of Abraham (Gal 3:7); for Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness, and he is the father of all them that believe, whether circumcised or uncircumcised (Rom 4:11). Thus John the Baptist warned the Pharisees not to boast, We have Abraham to our father, for God is able of stones to raise up children unto Abraham; and the Lord told Zacchaeus the publican, This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham—reckoning the repentant tax-gatherer a true heir of the promise. To be a son of Abraham in the saving sense is to walk in the steps of that faith which he had, trusting the God who justifies the ungodly. The dictionary honors the title as the charter of the gospel to the nations: that in Abraham’s seed, which is Christ, all the families of the earth are blessed, and every believer made an heir according to the promise.
webster_summary: A descendant of Abraham; more deeply, one who shares his faith. They which are of faith are the children of Abraham, heirs of the promise in Christ.
webster_full: SON OF ABRAHAM, a descendant of the patriarch; truly, an heir of his faith.
They which are of faith are the children of Abraham (Gal 3:7).
John warned the Pharisees not to boast of Abraham as their father.
Christ named Zacchaeus the publican a son of Abraham by repentance and faith.
In Abraham’s seed, Christ, all families of the earth are blessed.

Luk 19:9

corruption_summary: Sonship to Abraham is claimed by mere descent or by ethnic pride; Scripture reckons the true sons by the faith of Abraham, not the blood alone.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the ancient one the Baptist and the Lord both rebuked: the presumption that natural descent from Abraham secures the promise apart from faith. The Pharisees said, We have Abraham to our father; John answered that God could raise up children to Abraham from stones (Matt 3:9), and the Lord declared that the children of the devil, not of Abraham, are known by their works. Blood without faith does not make a true son.

The principle to recover is that sonship to Abraham is by faith, and so the title is the charter of the gospel to the nations. Abraham was justified by believing God before he was circumcised, that he might be the father of all who believe, Jew and Gentile alike (Rom 4:11). When the Lord called the repentant publican Zacchaeus a son of Abraham (Luke 19:9), He reckoned saving faith, not pedigree, as the mark of the true heir. Every believer in Christ, Abraham’s seed, is thereby a child of the patriarch and an heir according to the promise.
roots_summary: Son + Abraham; a descendant of the patriarch, and truly an heir of his faith—they which are of faith are the children of Abraham.

etymology: From Christ + the suffix -ian, belonging to; first given to the disciples at Antioch (Acts 11:26).
biblical_def: The name Christian means one who belongs to Christ, a follower and partisan of the Anointed One, and it was first given to the disciples at Antioch, where for a whole year Barnabas and Saul taught much people (Acts 11:26). The name appears only three times in the New Testament—at Antioch, on the lips of Agrippa, who told Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian, and in Peter’s charge that if any man suffer as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God on this behalf. Whether first coined by outsiders in derision or adopted by the disciples themselves, it became the honored name of the people of Christ, marking them as His possession, bearing His name as a wife bears her husband’s. To wear the name is no light thing: it binds the bearer to confess Christ, to suffer for Him without shame, and to depart from iniquity, that the name be not blasphemed. The dictionary honors the name Christian as the badge of belonging to the Lord, and warns that the name without the new birth, the title without the reality, profits nothing—for not every one that saith Lord, Lord, but he that doeth the will of the Father, shall enter the kingdom.
webster_summary: One who belongs to Christ; the name first given to the disciples at Antioch, marking them as His possession, to be borne in confession and without shame.
webster_full: CHRISTIAN, one who belongs to Christ; a follower of the Anointed.
First given to the disciples at Antioch (Act 11:26).
Appears thrice in the New Testament: Antioch, Agrippa, and Peter’s charge.
Marks the bearer as Christ’s possession, bearing His name.
The name without the new birth profits nothing.
scriptures: And when he had found him, he brought him unto Antioch. And it came to pass, that a whole year they assembled themselves with the church, and taught much people. And the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch.
Yet if any man suffer as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify God on this behalf.
Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian.
Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his. And, let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity.
corruption_summary: The name Christian is reduced to a cultural label or a nominal inheritance; Scripture binds it to belonging to Christ, confession, and a holy walk.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the hollowing of the name into a mere cultural or inherited label—Christian as a census category, a civic identity, or a family tradition, worn without the new birth or any living union with Christ. To bear the name of the Lord while a stranger to His grace is to take that name in vain; the name was never meant to be a label only, but the badge of those who are truly His.

The principle to recover is that the name binds its bearer to the reality it signifies. Peter charges that if any suffer as a Christian, he should not be ashamed but glorify God (1 Pet 4:16); Paul writes that every one who names the name of Christ must depart from iniquity (2 Tim 2:19). The name is a calling and a claim: it summons the bearer to confess Christ before men, to walk worthy of Him, and to count His reproach greater riches than the treasures of the world. The title without the reality the Lord Himself rejects: not every one that saith Lord, Lord, shall enter the kingdom.
roots_summary: Christ + -ian (belonging to); the name first given the disciples at Antioch, marking them as Christ’s own.
roots_lines: Christian — from Christ + -ian, belonging to Christ.
First given to the disciples at Antioch (Act 11:26).
Appears thrice in the New Testament; an honored badge of belonging.
To suffer as a Christian is no shame but God’s glory (1Pe 4:16).
The name binds its bearer to depart from iniquity (2Ti 2:19).
usage: The disciples were called Christians first in Antioch.
If any man suffer as a Christian, let him glorify God and not be ashamed.
The name without the new birth is a title worn in vain.

etymology: From household + God; a New Testament image of the church as the family and dwelling of God.
biblical_def: The household of God is a New Testament image of the church as the family and dwelling of God, a people no more strangers and foreigners but fellowcitizens with the saints and of the household of God (Eph 2:19). Paul tells Timothy how to behave himself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth (1 Tim 3:15). The image gathers up several truths: that believers are adopted as sons and made members of one family under one Father; that the church is built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ Himself being the chief corner stone, and grows unto an holy temple in the Lord, a habitation of God through the Spirit; and that God’s house has an order—officers, duties, and discipline—in which each member has a place and a charge. To be of the household of God is to belong, by adoption and the new birth, to the family of the Father, with Christ as elder brother and the saints as brethren. The dictionary honors this image as a chief glory of the church: not a mere institution or voluntary club, but the very house and family of the living God, where He dwells by His Spirit and where His children are nourished, ordered, and kept.
webster_summary: The church as the family and dwelling of God; believers made fellowcitizens and members of God’s house, built on Christ the corner stone, indwelt by the Spirit.
webster_full: HOUSEHOLD OF GOD, the church as the family and dwelling of God.
Believers are fellowcitizens with the saints, of God’s household (Eph 2:19).
The house of God is the church of the living God, pillar of the truth (1Ti 3:15).
Built on Christ the chief corner stone, a habitation of God through the Spirit.
A family by adoption, ordered with officers, duties, and discipline.
scriptures: Eph 2:19
Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God;
But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
Eph 2:22
In whom ye also are builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit.
Gal 6:10
As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.
corruption_summary: The church is reduced to a voluntary institution or a personal-preference club; the household image binds believers into God’s ordered family and dwelling.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the modern reduction of the church to a voluntary institution, a service-provider, or a club chosen by personal preference and left at will. The household image rebukes this. Believers are not customers but children, not members of a club but of a family, of the household of God (Eph 2:19), with duties to the Father and to one another that no consumer may set aside.

The principle to recover is the ordered, familial, and divine character of the church. Paul instructs Timothy how to behave in the house of God, the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth (1 Tim 3:15)—a house with officers, order, and discipline, not a formless gathering. Yet it is also a dwelling: builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit (Eph 2:22). To belong to the household of God is therefore to be at once a child loved by the Father and a member bound to His order, doing good especially to them who are of the household of faith (Gal 6:10).
roots_summary: Household + God; the church as the family and dwelling of God, built on Christ the corner stone and indwelt by the Spirit.
roots_lines: Household of God — the church as God’s family and dwelling.
Believers are fellowcitizens and of God’s household (Eph 2:19).
The house of God is the church, the pillar of the truth (1Ti 3:15).
A habitation of God through the Spirit (Eph 2:22).
An ordered family with officers, duties, and discipline.
usage: Believers are no more strangers but of the household of God.
Paul taught Timothy how to behave in the house of the living God.
We do good especially unto them who are of the household of faith.

etymology: From church + firstborn; the general assembly of the redeemed, written in heaven (Heb 12:23).
biblical_def: The church of the firstborn is the whole company of the redeemed, named in the great vision of Hebrews 12, where the writer tells believers that they are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels, to the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven (Heb 12:22-23). The title carries the dignity of the firstborn—the heir, the one who receives the inheritance and the double portion—and applies it to all the saints, who in Christ the firstborn among many brethren are made joint-heirs, their names enrolled in heaven. It speaks of the church not chiefly as the visible congregation on earth but as the one redeemed assembly of all ages gathered around the throne, the church triumphant and militant joined in one. To belong to the church of the firstborn is to have one’s name written in heaven, to be an heir of the eternal inheritance through union with Christ the firstborn, and to be already, by faith, come to that heavenly city. The dictionary honors this title as a crown of the doctrine of the church: the redeemed are not a scattered remnant of the despised but the enrolled heirs of God, the firstborn sons gathered to the city that hath foundations.
webster_summary: The whole company of the redeemed, heirs in Christ the firstborn, whose names are written in heaven; the one assembly gathered to the heavenly Jerusalem.
webster_full: CHURCH OF THE FIRSTBORN, the whole company of the redeemed (Heb 12:23).
Believers are come to the general assembly and church of the firstborn.
Bears the dignity of the firstborn: the heir of the inheritance.
In Christ the firstborn among many brethren, the saints are joint-heirs.
Their names are written in heaven, enrolled as the sons of God.
scriptures: To the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven, and to God the Judge of all, and to the spirits of just men made perfect,
But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels,
Rom 8:29
For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.
Notwithstanding in this rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven.
corruption_summary: The church is shrunk to a local institution or a sociological body; the church of the firstborn lifts the eye to the one redeemed assembly enrolled in heaven.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the shrinking of the church to a merely earthly, sociological, or institutional body—a denomination, a building, a local roll of members—forgetting the larger reality. The church of the firstborn names the one redeemed assembly of all ages, the church militant and triumphant joined, already gathered by faith to the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 12:22-23). The visible congregation is real and to be loved, but it is the local outcropping of a far greater company.

The principle to recover is the heavenly dignity and security of the redeemed. To be of the church of the firstborn is to share the inheritance of Christ, the firstborn among many brethren (Rom 8:29), and to have one’s name written in heaven (Luke 10:20)—a cause of deeper rejoicing than any earthly power or success. The doctrine lifts the suffering saint’s eyes from his small and afflicted congregation to the innumerable company around the throne, and assures him that his name, by grace, is already enrolled among the firstborn heirs of God.
roots_summary: Church + firstborn; the whole redeemed assembly, heirs in Christ the firstborn, whose names are written in heaven (Heb 12:23).
roots_lines: Church of the firstborn — the whole company of the redeemed.
Believers are come to this general assembly (Heb 12:23).
Bears the firstborn’s dignity: the heir of the inheritance.
In Christ the firstborn among many brethren (Rom 8:29).
Their names are written in heaven (Luk 10:20).
usage: Believers are come to the general assembly and church of the firstborn.
In Christ the firstborn, the saints are joint-heirs of the inheritance.
Rejoice rather that your names are written in heaven.
